## How can you tell if a Reddit post is AI?

This data can't tell you whether any single post is AI. It shows how often popular signs appear. Of the 26 I measured, only the em dash is clearly more common in January to September 2026 than in the same months of 2019 to 2022.

If you've ever wondered how to tell if a Reddit post is AI, you've probably seen the list. The word "delve". The word "tapestry". "It's not just X, it's Y." Headings, bold labels and emoji bullet points. And the em dash, always the em dash.

These are signs I keep seeing named in guides and threads about AI writing. I've counted how often Reddit comments say AI slop . Do they really show up more in Reddit posts now than before ChatGPT?

So I took 5,253,515 text posts from 100 large subreddits. Those are the text posts with a real body of text that were still visible in the data, leaving out known bots and posts by accounts that had been deleted, from the first nine months of each year before ChatGPT came out, and from the same months of 2026. An estimated quarter (25.0%) of the posts the older years would hold if captured as in 2026 are missing, and "What this data can't tell you" explains why. For each sign I asked one narrow question. How much more or less common is it in 2026 than before?

There's a catch, though. Language drifts. Any word can get more or less common over a few years, as the 40 random words show, and the mix of subreddits shifts too. So I didn't just ask whether a sign went up. I also picked 40 words of moderate frequency at random, like "barber", "ibuprofen" and "parlor", and measured how far they moved. A sign only counts as rising if it clearly moved further than those words. Think of them as the background noise of a language that keeps changing. I set this rule after seeing the first results. Under the band the plan fixed, built from three control words and wide (0.9× to 1.7×), "in conclusion" would have counted as a real fall. I added a narrower within-subreddit band built from three control words (about 1.0× to 1.1×) while analysing. With it 7 other signs would have counted as rising and 5 as falling.

## Is the em dash a sign of AI on Reddit?

It's the only sign here that clearly grew. In January to September 2026, 5.12% of text posts of 200+ characters in 100 large subreddits had an em dash in the body, up from 0.69% in the same months of 2019 to 2022, about 7 times the old rate. That still doesn't make any one post with an em dash AI.

I tried to break this result, and it held each time:

- Comparing posts within each subreddit, so a shift in which subreddits post more can't explain it: 5.4×.

- Comparing the same summer months of 2023 and 2026, when posts were probably captured in a similar way (I assume the way posts are captured changed in mid-2023 and did not check month by month): 6.1×.

- Leaving out r/MakeNewFriendsHere , which makes up a much bigger share of the posts in 2026: 7.1×.

- Assuming the posts missing from the older years used em dashes three times as often as the rest: 4.9×.

But look at when it happened:

Source: KissMyPost analysis of 13,219,288 public Reddit text posts of 200+ characters in 100 subreddits, January 2019 to September 2026.

Not much happened when ChatGPT launched: the em dash rate in January to September 2023 was only 1.1× the old one, and the interval includes no change at all. Then it climbed, with jumps in August 2024 and April 2025. So if you're thinking "ChatGPT came out, em dashes went up", the timing doesn't back you up. The em dash share of text posts rose long after ChatGPT launched; this data can't say what drove it.

I've written about the em dash on Reddit on its own, with comments too. The title-or-body version matches that study almost exactly (5.49% and 5.48% for the first quarter of 2026); the headline numbers here count the body only.

Does it depend on how long the post is? Here's the same ratio by length:

Source: KissMyPost analysis of 5,253,515 public Reddit text posts of 200+ characters in 100 subreddits.

Short posts came in at 9.1× and long ones at 4.1×. That looks like a big gap. But the two intervals overlap a little, so I can't say the short ones really changed more.

## Which AI phrases and words got more common on Reddit?

None cleared the bar in the main comparison. "In today's fast-paced/digital/world" came out at 2.3×, and "it's not just X, it's Y" at 1.8×. But random words got that high too, so I can't separate those from drift.

Before I ran the numbers, I wrote down that "delve", "tapestry" and "testament to" would be at least twice as common in 2026. "Delve" (1.0×) and "testament to" (1.1×) weren't. "Tapestry" came out at 1.9×, but with about a hundred posts per window the interval can't settle it.

The famous words tell a different story if you go year by year. In 2024, "delve" was above its old rate (2.3×), but I did not test that against random-word drift in 2024. "Tapestry" was above its old rate the year before (4.9×), and I did not test that either. Then "delve" came back to its old rate:

Source: KissMyPost analysis of 13,219,288 public Reddit text posts of 200+ characters in 100 subreddits. Intervals are in the CSV files.

By this year "delve" was back to 1.0× in the main comparison (0.7× within each subreddit, 0.4× in the summer version), so roughly where it started or lower. "Tapestry" is harder to call. It's rarer than you might think: only 108 posts used it in the four baseline periods against 103 in January to September 2026. With counts that small, the year-by-year intervals overlap. The summer-to-summer version (0.3×) points down but sits inside the drift band, so I can't call it a real fall.

How high "delve" went depends partly on one subreddit, as the 1.8× without r/MakeNewFriendsHere shows. "Let's dive in" and "let's break it down" were already 5.7× their old rate in 2023 and 7.4× in 2024 (the intervals overlap), 5.0× in 2025 and 1.6× in 2026.

Month by month, you can see the bump in "delve" start in the spring of 2023 and fade through 2025:

"It's not just X, it's Y" moved the other way, edging up through 2025. October 2025 looks odd here too, as in my em dash study. Even so, its ratio this year is inside the random-word range. In the version of this pattern that also accepts a dash, the within-subreddit ratio (2.1×) goes beyond the random-word range; see Method. And I only counted posts that fit a pattern. I didn't check how many matches of the pattern are the construction itself, so if you've spotted the real thing in the wild, you've seen something this count can't confirm.

## Which supposed AI tells did not clearly change?

In posts, "hope this helps" stayed about where it was: 0.07% of posts before ChatGPT and 0.06% in 2026. "Great question" is too rare to say much, with 77 posts in 2019 to 2022 and 53 in 2026, and the versions of the comparison disagree (0.6× to 7.6×); the 7.6× in the summer version rests on very few posts. Both are mostly things people say in replies (my assumption), and comments weren't measured.

The transition words didn't rise either. "Moreover", "furthermore", "additionally" and "it's worth noting" all came in at or below their old rates. "In conclusion" showed up about half as often in 2026 (0.5×).

That looks like a real drop, but random words fell that far too. The lowest of the 40 came in at 0.4×. So I'd rather not read anything into it. Here are the transition words year by year:

Source: KissMyPost analysis of 13,219,288 public Reddit text posts of 200+ characters in 100 subreddits.

For scale, the plain word "because" sat at about 23% of posts, before and after. Next to that, every one of these phrases is rare. You could read a thousand posts and meet "in conclusion" once or not at all.

## Did headings, bold text and emoji lists get more common?

Headings and bold labels in lists jumped from the second quarter of 2024 and headings kept rising until the first quarter of 2025, partly overlapping with a zero-width-space code vanishing from posts. When the code returned in 2026, headings did not fall. That code may be an editor leftover, but I couldn't confirm it, so I don't count them as signs that rose.

Here's the jump, quarter by quarter:

Source: KissMyPost analysis of public Reddit text posts of 200+ characters in 100 subreddits, from 2022 to September 2026.

And here's the zero-width-space code over the same quarters:

The code fell from 5.4% of posts to 0.06% in two quarters. It came back this year with a spike I can't explain, so I'm leaving that as an open question.

I'd also guessed, before looking, that bold text and bold labels would grow more than any of the words. They didn't, at least not clearly. Emoji lists were already on the rise before ChatGPT came out: 0.05% of posts in 2019 and 0.29% in 2022, and the intervals don't overlap, so their ratio says little about AI. Bold text went from 3.45% to 4.27% of posts, but that is inside the range of random words, so I can't tell it from drift. This data can't say whether it's a giveaway.

## How many Reddit posts have any of the 20 word, phrase and formatting signs?

Very few. In January to September 2026, 94.6% of Reddit text posts in 100 large subreddits contained none of 20 signs (10 words, 6 phrases and 4 formatting habits; the em dash and the 5 transition words not counted). In January to September 2019 to 2022 it was 95.6%. The em dash alone is in 5.12%.

So whatever these signs mean, you'll only meet them in a small slice of posts. I also don't add them up into a score. Bold labels in lists are also bold text, so one formatting habit can count twice, and I don't report the share of posts with two or more signs.
